transcript.content: Hello, welcome. What brings you in to see me today?

I'm here because for the last year and seven months, I've been dealing with this overwhelming surge of energy and extreme mood swings. I keep shifting between feeling incredibly high and on top of the world, to being intensely irritable and angry at the smallest things. It's just exhausting because my mood is constantly bouncing back and forth like this.
During those times when you feel incredibly high or on top of the world, has this ever caused major disruptions in your daily life or work, or have you ever needed to be hospitalized because of it?

Yes, these high periods have caused major disruptions over the past year and seven months, especially since my reckless spending and foolish business investments have put me in severe financial distress. However, I have never been hospitalized because of it.
During these high periods, or even when your mood feels normal, have you ever heard voices, seen things others couldn't, or had strong beliefs that other people found highly unusual?
No, I've never heard any voices or seen things that weren't really there. I also haven't held any unusual beliefs that other people found strange.
Have you ever experienced periods lasting two weeks or more where you felt consistently sad, down, or lost interest in almost all of your usual activities?
No, I haven't really experienced anything like that. I don't recall ever feeling consistently sad or losing interest in my usual activities for weeks at a time.

latest_inference.note: Previously, the candidates were Bipolar I Disorder and Bipolar II Disorder. Bipolar II Disorder is now ruled out because the patient has never experienced a major depressive episode, which is a required criterion for Bipolar II. Furthermore, the patient's high periods have caused marked impairment (major disruptions and severe financial distress due to reckless spending), which meets the criteria for a manic episode rather than a hypomanic episode, confirming a diagnosis of Bipolar I Disorder.
